title: Does Science Disprove God?
excerpt: The war between science and faith is a story told in the nineteenth century, and Galileo and Darwin both went differently than the story says. Science has made one kind of god unnecessary. Whether it can rule on the God of the creeds is a different question.
body:
A girl in the tenth grade loves her biology class and loves her church, and in the same month a youth leader and a teacher each tell her, from opposite directions, that she will eventually have to pick one. A physician stopped believing somewhere in his second year of medical school. He cannot remember deciding to. It was more that the question stopped coming up. And a retired engineer in the third pew has quietly concluded that scientists know less than they claim and say more than they know, because that is the only way he can see to keep his Bible.

All three have accepted the same picture, in which there are two sides and a person stands on one of them. The picture is younger than it looks, and most of the history it appeals to went differently.

## The Charge

The charge comes in two forms, and the famous one is the weaker.

The famous form is a war. In 1874 the chemist John William Draper published a history built on one sentence: "The history of Science is not a mere record of isolated discoveries; it is a narrative of the conflict of two contending powers, the expansive force of the human intellect on one side, and the compression arising from traditionary faith and human interests on the other." Galileo on his knees is the center of that story, and Darwin is its second act.

The quieter form needs no war at all. It needs only a track record. For most of history a storm, an epidemic or an eclipse was read as the act of a god, and one by one those readings gave way to natural explanations that could be tested and that worked. Then, in 1859, Charles Darwin offered a natural explanation of the hardest case, which was how living things come to be so well suited to the way they live. He described the effect on his own mind years later: "The old argument from design in Nature, as given by Paley, which formerly seemed to me so conclusive, fails, now that the law of natural selection has been discovered." On this telling God was never refuted. He was simply needed for less and less, until a fair-minded person could wonder whether he had ever been more than a name for what was not yet understood.

## Galileo

The core of the Galileo story is true, and Christians gain nothing by trimming it. As this site's page on [Galileo and the war](/questions/science/galileo-and-the-war) sets out, Rome's theologians judged in 1616 that a sun standing still at the center of the world was "formally heretical," and in 1633 the Inquisition declared Galileo "vehemently suspected of heresy." He was made to renounce the earth's motion on his knees. His book was banned, he lived under house arrest until he died in 1642, and the book did not come off the church's list of forbidden reading until 1835. The verses used against him included the day Joshua prayed and "the sun stood still" (Joshua 10:13).

What the legend added is another matter. Galileo was not an unbeliever attacking the church from outside. He was a Christian who argued that the Bible describes the sky the way ordinary people see it, and he called a witness from the church's own bench. Augustine had warned, twelve centuries earlier, that when an outsider catches a Christian saying foolish things about nature it is "a disgraceful and dangerous thing." Nor was the science finished in 1633. The telescope had badly damaged the old earth-centered system, but the direct measurement that shows the earth moving against the stars was not made until 1838. And the same page reports that historians have found no evidence that Galileo was tortured, and that apart from a few days he was never kept in a prison cell.

None of that excuses the sentence. The judges mistook their reading of the Bible for the Bible. Scripture says that "the sun rises, and the sun goes down" (Ecclesiastes 1:5), and so does every weather forecast, and nobody takes either for a statement about orbits. The church had the means to know better, in its own best teacher, and it punished the man who reminded it.

## Darwin

The second act went even less like a war. Darwin opened *On the Origin of Species* with a quotation from Francis Bacon, urging that no one "think or maintain, that a man can search too far or be too well studied in the book of God's word, or in the book of God's works." The first edition closed with life "having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one." In later editions Darwin made it "originally breathed by the Creator." He also added a line from a clergyman who had written to him that it was "just as noble a conception of the Deity to believe that He created a few original forms capable of self-development."

Darwin's own faith did fade, and he said how. "Disbelief crept over me at a very slow rate, but was at last complete," he wrote of Christianity. The reasons he listed were mostly a historian's reasons, and he dated them to the late 1830s, twenty years before his book: doubts about the Old Testament, about when the Gospels were written and how they differ, and about miracles in a world of fixed laws. Even then he refused the label later pinned on him. "In my most extreme fluctuations I have never been an Atheist in the sense of denying the existence of a God," he wrote in 1879. He preferred another word: "The mystery of the beginning of all things is insoluble by us; and I for one must be content to remain an Agnostic."

The churches did not answer with one voice. Some preachers attacked the book and some welcomed it, and Darwin's chief defender in America, the botanist Asa Gray, was a convinced Christian. The trial everyone remembers came two generations later, in a Tennessee courtroom in 1925. This site's history course notes what the usual telling leaves out: the famous politician who spoke for the prosecution feared the theory mainly for the social ruthlessness then being drawn from it, and the textbook at issue taught eugenics. Neither side of that courtroom was simply right.

## What Science Can Rule On

Science explains one state of the natural world by another, and it has a rule that makes it work: look for natural causes, test what you find, and let the results correct you. Nobody doing chemistry may enter a miracle in the results column. Believing scientists have honored that rule as strictly as their unbelieving colleagues, and where the church has tried to overrule a measurement with a verse, the church has lost and has deserved to.

The same rule sets the limits. A method built to study how nature behaves cannot tell anyone why there is a nature, or why it runs on laws, or why creatures who grew up inside it can read those laws in mathematics. It cannot weigh a promise, or say what a human being is worth. It cannot rule on whether, once, something happened that the regular course of nature does not account for, since the regular course of nature is all it measures. Those questions are real ones. They belong to philosophy and to history, and a scientist who answers them is doing philosophy or history when he does, sometimes well.

So the quiet form of the charge is right about one kind of god. A god who lives in the gaps of present knowledge gets smaller every time a gap closes, and the church has often leaned on him. The pastor Dietrich Bonhoeffer saw this from a prison cell in 1944. As the site's page on [whether science has made God unnecessary](/questions/science/has-science-made-god-unnecessary) quotes him, "We are to find God in what we know, not in what we don't know."

The God of the creeds was never that god. Thomas Aquinas raised the modern objection against himself in the thirteenth century, in nearly modern words: since everything in the world can be traced to natural causes or to human choices, "there is no need to suppose God's existence." His answer was that nature's own working has to be accounted for: "whatever is done by nature must needs be traced back to God, as to its first cause." On that view God does not compete with natural causes for a share of the explaining. He is the reason there are natural causes. Paul says it of Christ: "in him all things hold together" (Colossians 1:17). If that is what Christians mean, then no finding about how the world works can be evidence against it, and none can prove it either.

## The Unbeliever's Best Case

That last admission is where the thoughtful unbeliever presses, and he should be heard.

A God who makes no difference a laboratory could detect, he says, begins to look like a God who makes no difference. Questions keep moving from the theologian's desk to the scientist's bench, and the traffic runs one way. Science has a built-in way of catching its own errors and uses it constantly. Religion, he says, has no such habit. And if the universe needs a reason, the reason needs one too. It is simpler to stop a step earlier. The philosopher Bertrand Russell said it in a radio debate in 1948: "I should say that the universe is just there, and that's all."

Much of this should be granted. The track record is real. Believers have defended mistakes long after the evidence was in. A person who is willing to take an orderly universe as a bare fact, with nothing behind it, is not being irrational, and the site's page says so.

## The Believer's Best Case

The scientist who believes has a case as well, and it does not depend on any gap.

It begins with the oddity that science works. Albert Einstein, no believer in a personal God, said in an essay of 1936 that "the eternal mystery of the world is its comprehensibility." The physicist Eugene Wigner called the power of mathematics to describe the physical world "a wonderful gift which we neither understand nor deserve." Neither man was arguing for God. Both saw that science rests on something it does not explain: an ordered world, and minds able to follow the order. Christians have a reason to expect both. Many who built the sciences had exactly that expectation. The doors of the laboratory that James Clerk Maxwell opened at Cambridge in the 1870s carried a line from the Psalms, put there in Latin at his request: "Great are the works of the LORD, studied by all who delight in them" (Psalm 111:2). The founder of genetics was a friar. One of the first physicists to argue that the universe is expanding, and that it had a beginning, was a priest.

Darwin felt the pull of this himself. He wrote of "the extreme difficulty or rather impossibility of conceiving this immense and wonderful universe" as "the result of blind chance or necessity," and added that when he thought this way, "I deserve to be called a Theist." Then he doubted his own conclusion. Could a mind descended from the lower animals be trusted on so large a question? The doubt is a fair one, and it cuts in every direction, since the same mind produced the theory.

The believer's case proves no more than the unbeliever's does. It shows that the success of science fits comfortably inside belief in a Creator, and that the people who built science knew it.

## Where Christians Differ

None of this settles the questions that divide Christians from one another, and this essay does not try to.

On the age of the earth, some hold that the six days of Genesis were days as we know them and that the world is young. Others hold that the days stand for long ages, and others that they are a literary frame, or God's workweek told by analogy, or the dedication of the world as a temple. On the history of life, some hold that God created the kinds of living things directly, some that he brought them about through the long development biologists trace, and some argue that features of life point to design. On Adam, many keep the view most Christians have held down the centuries, that he and Eve were a first pair and the ancestors of everyone. Others hold that they were real persons within a larger population, and others read them as a figure for every human being. On the flood, some hold that it covered the globe, some that it covered the world Noah knew, and some that Genesis tells a real memory in the forms of its time.

Each of these has defenders who recite the same creeds, and each has a difficulty its best defenders admit. For some the difficulty is the evidence of the sciences, which nearly all who work in them read as showing a very old earth and a shared ancestry of living things. For others it is the text of Genesis and Paul's argument about Adam and death. The site sets the positions out, with the hardest question for each, on its pages about [the age of the earth](/questions/science/how-old-is-the-earth), [evolution and Genesis](/questions/science/evolution-and-genesis), [Adam and Eve](/questions/science/adam-eve-and-human-origins) and [the flood](/questions/old-testament/the-flood-and-babylon), and it takes no side. Neither does this essay. One sentence from those pages is worth carrying away: "A Christian who changes her mind about the age of the earth hasn't changed her religion."

## What We Have Done

The church's part in this confusion is larger than the trial of 1633.

We have told the young that they must choose, and we have said it from pulpits as confidently as any skeptic has said it from a lectern. A student who is taught that her faith stands or falls with one reading of Genesis will let go of both together if she ever lets go of the reading, and many have. We have hinted that scientists are hiding what they know, which is a charge against real people and ought to come with evidence. We have rested the faith on gaps and then been surprised when the gaps closed.

We have also done the opposite, and it flatters us more. Some of us have been so eager to stand well with educated opinion that we would trade away any miracle to keep our seat at the table, the resurrection included. That is no peace between faith and science. It gives up the faith and calls the result peace.

## What Is Settled and What Is Not

Christians confess that God is the maker of heaven and earth and of everything in them, that human beings bear his image, and that the world's order is his gift. "By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God" (Hebrews 11:3). The creeds say nothing of how long the making took or by what means.

The age of the earth, the history of life, the details about Adam and the extent of the flood are questions on which faithful churches differ.

Science has not disproved God, and it could not. Nor has it proved him. Its method is not built for either task. Where Christianity can be tested is in a claim about one man in one city in one decade, and Paul admitted that if it fails, the rest goes with it: "if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:14). That is a matter for historians, and this site has [an essay on the resurrection](/writing/did-the-resurrection-happen) that takes it up.

So nobody had the right to tell the girl in the tenth grade to choose. She can take every hour of biology her school offers, and she will find that the Christians who came before her in that work were not embarrassed by it. The engineer owes the scientists the same fairness he would want for himself. The physician might notice that his faith went the way Darwin's did, slowly and without distress, and that Darwin's own account of his has very little biology in it. A faith can lapse without ever having been answered.

Galileo's telescope helped to settle a question about the planets. It was never able to settle who made them, and the people who thought it could were on both sides of the courtroom.

*"Great are the works of the LORD, studied by all who delight in them."* (Psalm 111:2)

*"It is the glory of God to conceal things, but the glory of kings is to search things out."* (Proverbs 25:2)
